Orion.name: Orion
Orion.description: Orion is one of the most recognizable constellations in the night sky. Named after a hunter in Greek mythology, it features some of the brightest stars including Betelgeuse and Rigel. The three stars forming Orion's Belt are among the most famous asterisms in astronomy.
Orion.history: In Greek mythology, Orion was a giant huntsman whom Zeus placed among the stars. Ancient Egyptians associated these stars with Osiris, the god of the afterlife. The constellation has been recognized across many cultures throughout history.
Orion.best_viewing: Winter (December to March in Northern Hemisphere)
Orion.notable_features: Orion's Belt, Orion Nebula (M42), Betelgeuse (red supergiant), Rigel (blue supergiant)

UMa.name: Ursa Major
UMa.description: Ursa Major is a prominent constellation visible throughout the year in most of the northern hemisphere. Its most famous feature is the Big Dipper asterism, which many use to find Polaris, the North Star.
UMa.history: In Greek mythology, Ursa Major represents Callisto, who was transformed into a bear by Zeus's jealous wife Hera. Native American tribes saw it as a bear being chased by hunters. It's one of the oldest named constellations.
UMa.notable_features: Big Dipper asterism, Mizar and Alcor (double star), pointer stars to Polaris

Cas.name: Cassiopeia
Cas.description: Cassiopeia is a distinctive W-shaped constellation in the northern sky. Named after the vain queen in Greek mythology, it's circumpolar for most northern observers, meaning it never sets below the horizon.
Cas.history: In mythology, Cassiopeia was the wife of King Cepheus and mother of Andromeda. Her boastfulness angered the sea nymphs, leading to her being placed in the sky where she must circle the celestial pole, sometimes hanging upside down.
Cas.notable_features: W or M shape, contains several open clusters including M52 and M103

Leo.name: Leo
Leo.description: Leo is a prominent zodiac constellation representing a lion. Its distinctive sickle shape marks the lion's head and mane, while Regulus, one of the brightest stars, represents the lion's heart.
Leo.history: Associated with the Nemean Lion slain by Hercules in Greek mythology. Ancient Egyptians worshipped it as the location where the sun appeared during the flooding of the Nile. It's been recognized as a lion across many ancient cultures.
Leo.notable_features: Regulus (the heart), the Sickle asterism, Leo Triplet galaxies (M65, M66, NGC 3628)

Cyg.name: Cygnus
Cyg.description: Cygnus represents a swan in flight, but its cross-like pattern also gives it the name 'Northern Cross'. It flies along the Milky Way, making it rich in deep-sky objects.
Cyg.history: In Greek mythology, the constellation represents several different swans. Most commonly, it's associated with the story of Zeus disguising himself as a swan. The Chinese saw it as part of a magpie bridge in the tale of star-crossed lovers.
Cyg.notable_features: Deneb (one of the brightest stars), Northern Cross asterism, Cygnus X-1 (black hole), North America Nebula

Sco.name: Scorpius
Sco.description: Scorpius is a zodiac constellation representing a scorpion. Its J-shaped pattern with the bright red star Antares at its heart is easily recognizable in the southern sky.
Sco.history: In Greek mythology, Scorpius was the scorpion sent by Gaia to kill the hunter Orion. This is why the two constellations are never visible together - as one rises, the other sets. Ancient Sumerians called it the 'creature with the burning sting'.
Sco.best_viewing: Summer (June to August in Northern Hemisphere)
Sco.notable_features: Antares (red supergiant 'rival of Mars'), rich star clusters including M4 and M80, lies in the direction of the galactic center

Tau.name: Taurus
Tau.description: Taurus is a prominent zodiac constellation representing a charging bull. It contains two of the nearest open star clusters: the Pleiades and the Hyades.
Tau.history: Associated with the bull form taken by Zeus to abduct Europa in Greek mythology. Ancient cultures from Mesopotamia to Egypt recognized this constellation, often as a bull. The Pleiades cluster within it has been noted by civilizations worldwide.
Tau.notable_features: Aldebaran (orange giant eye), Pleiades (Seven Sisters), Hyades cluster, Crab Nebula (M1)

Gem.name: Gemini
Gem.description: Gemini represents the twins Castor and Pollux from Greek mythology. Two bright stars bearing their names mark the heads of the twins.
Gem.history: In Greek mythology, Castor and Pollux were twin half-brothers. Pollux was immortal while Castor was mortal. When Castor died, Pollux asked Zeus to let him share his immortality, and they were placed together in the sky.
Gem.notable_features: Castor (six-star system), Pollux (closest giant star to Earth), location of 1930 discovery of Pluto

Vir.name: Virgo
Vir.description: Virgo is the second-largest constellation and a member of the zodiac. It contains the Virgo Cluster, one of the closest galaxy clusters to the Milky Way.
Vir.history: Often associated with Persephone, daughter of Demeter, or with the goddess of justice Astraea. The constellation has been linked to harvest goddesses across many ancient cultures, appearing in the sky during harvest season.
Vir.notable_features: Spica (bright blue star), Virgo Cluster of galaxies (over 2000 galaxies), home to many Messier objects

Aqr.name: Aquarius
Aqr.description: Aquarius is a zodiac constellation representing a person pouring water from a jar. Despite its size, it contains no particularly bright stars.
Aqr.history: Associated with Ganymede in Greek mythology, a beautiful youth taken to Olympus to serve as Zeus's cup-bearer. Many ancient cultures saw it as water-related due to its appearance during the rainy season.
Aqr.notable_features: Saturn Nebula, Helix Nebula (closest planetary nebula), several meteor showers radiate from this region

And.name: Andromeda
And.description: Andromeda represents the princess from Greek mythology who was chained to a rock as a sacrifice. It's most famous for containing the Andromeda Galaxy.
And.history: In Greek mythology, Andromeda was the daughter of Cassiopeia and Cepheus. She was chained as a sacrifice to appease Poseidon but was rescued by Perseus. All these characters appear as neighboring constellations.
And.notable_features: Andromeda Galaxy (M31 - nearest major galaxy), Alpheratz (shared with Pegasus), Blue Snowball Nebula

Per.name: Perseus
Per.description: Perseus represents the Greek hero who slayed Medusa and rescued Andromeda. It's a prominent constellation in the northern winter sky.
Per.history: Named after the legendary Greek hero Perseus, son of Zeus. The constellation depicts him holding the head of Medusa, represented by the famous variable star Algol, known as the 'Demon Star'.
Per.notable_features: Algol (eclipsing binary 'Demon Star'), Double Cluster (NGC 869 and 884), Perseid meteor shower radiant

Andromeda.name: Andromeda
Andromeda.description: Andromeda represents the princess from Greek mythology who was chained to a rock as a sacrifice. It's most famous for containing the Andromeda Galaxy.
Andromeda.history: In Greek mythology, Andromeda was the daughter of Cassiopeia and Cepheus. She was chained as a sacrifice to appease Poseidon but was rescued by Perseus. All these characters appear as neighboring constellations.
Andromeda.notable_features: Andromeda Galaxy (M31 - nearest major galaxy), Alpheratz (shared with Pegasus), Blue Snowball Nebula

Perseus.name: Perseus
Perseus.description: Perseus represents the Greek hero who slayed Medusa and rescued Andromeda. It's a prominent constellation in the northern winter sky.
Perseus.history: Named after the legendary Greek hero Perseus, son of Zeus. The constellation depicts him holding the head of Medusa, represented by the famous variable star Algol, known as the 'Demon Star'.
Perseus.notable_features: Algol (eclipsing binary 'Demon Star'), Double Cluster (NGC 869 and 884), Perseid meteor shower radiant

Cygnus.name: Cygnus
Cygnus.description: Cygnus represents a swan in flight, but its cross-like pattern also gives it the name 'Northern Cross'. It flies along the Milky Way, making it rich in deep-sky objects.
Cygnus.history: In Greek mythology, the constellation represents several different swans. Most commonly, it's associated with the story of Zeus disguising himself as a swan. The Chinese saw it as part of a magpie bridge in the tale of star-crossed lovers.
Cygnus.notable_features: Deneb (one of the brightest stars), Northern Cross asterism, Cygnus X-1 (black hole), North America Nebula

Cassiopeia.name: Cassiopeia
Cassiopeia.description: Cassiopeia is a distinctive W-shaped constellation in the northern sky. Named after the vain queen in Greek mythology, it's circumpolar for most northern observers, meaning it never sets below the horizon.
Cassiopeia.history: In mythology, Cassiopeia was the wife of King Cepheus and mother of Andromeda. Her boastfulness angered the sea nymphs, leading to her being placed in the sky where she must circle the celestial pole, sometimes hanging upside down.
Cassiopeia.notable_features: W or M shape, contains several open clusters including M52 and M103

Monoceros.name: Monoceros
Monoceros.description: Monoceros is a faint constellation on the celestial equator, representing a mythical unicorn. It lies in the area surrounded by Orion, Canis Major, and Canis Minor.
Monoceros.history: Unlike most constellations, Monoceros doesn't have ancient origins. It was created by Dutch cartographer Petrus Plancius in 1612 and later included in Johann Bayer's star atlas. Despite its faintness, it's rich in deep-sky objects due to its location in the Milky Way.
Monoceros.notable_features: Rosette Nebula, Christmas Tree Cluster, Cone Nebula, several open clusters including M50

UrsaMajor.name: Ursa Major
UrsaMajor.description: Ursa Major is a prominent constellation visible throughout the year in most of the northern hemisphere. Its most famous feature is the Big Dipper asterism, which many use to find Polaris, the North Star.
UrsaMajor.history: In Greek mythology, Ursa Major represents Callisto, who was transformed into a bear by Zeus's jealous wife Hera. Native American tribes saw it as a bear being chased by hunters. It's one of the oldest named constellations.
UrsaMajor.notable_features: Big Dipper asterism, Mizar and Alcor (double star), pointer stars to Polaris

Pegasus.name: Pegasus
Pegasus.description: Pegasus is a prominent constellation in the northern autumn sky, known for its distinctive square asterism. It represents the mythical winged horse from Greek mythology.
Pegasus.history: In Greek mythology, Pegasus was born from the blood of Medusa when Perseus beheaded her. The winged horse became the companion of heroes and eventually was placed among the stars by Zeus.
Pegasus.notable_features: Great Square of Pegasus asterism, Stephan's Quintet galaxy group, several globular clusters

CanisMajor.name: Canis Major
CanisMajor.description: Canis Major represents the larger of Orion's two hunting dogs. It contains Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky.
CanisMajor.history: In Greek mythology, Canis Major is one of Orion's hunting dogs. Various cultures have seen it as a dog or wolf. The ancient Egyptians associated Sirius with the goddess Isis and the flooding of the Nile.
CanisMajor.notable_features: Sirius (brightest star), several open clusters including M41

CanisMinor.name: Canis Minor
CanisMinor.description: Canis Minor is a small constellation representing the smaller of Orion's two hunting dogs. Despite its size, it contains the bright star Procyon.
CanisMinor.history: Like Canis Major, this constellation represents one of Orion's hunting dogs in Greek mythology. It's been recognized as a dog across many ancient cultures.
CanisMinor.notable_features: Procyon (8th brightest star in the sky), forms the Winter Triangle with Sirius and Betelgeuse

UrsaMinor.name: Ursa Minor
UrsaMinor.description: Ursa Minor contains Polaris, the North Star, at the end of its tail. The Little Dipper asterism is part of this constellation.
UrsaMinor.history: In Greek mythology, Ursa Minor represents Arcas, son of Callisto (Ursa Major). Various cultures have used this constellation for navigation due to Polaris.
UrsaMinor.notable_features: Polaris (North Star), Little Dipper asterism, circumpolar for northern observers

Aquila.name: Aquila
Aquila.description: Aquila represents an eagle in flight. Its brightest star, Altair, forms one vertex of the Summer Triangle.
Aquila.history: In Greek mythology, Aquila carried Zeus's thunderbolts. It was also the eagle that carried Ganymede to Olympus to serve as Zeus's cup-bearer.
Aquila.notable_features: Altair (one of the closest naked-eye stars), part of Summer Triangle, lies in the Milky Way

Lyra.name: Lyra
Lyra.description: Lyra represents the lyre of Orpheus. Despite being small, it contains Vega, one of the brightest stars in the sky.
Lyra.history: In Greek mythology, this was the lyre given to Orpheus by Apollo. When Orpheus died, Zeus placed the lyre among the stars.
Lyra.notable_features: Vega (5th brightest star), Ring Nebula (M57), part of Summer Triangle

Auriga.name: Auriga
Auriga.description: Auriga is a pentagon-shaped constellation containing the bright star Capella. It represents a charioteer in Greek mythology.
Auriga.history: Associated with various characters in mythology, most commonly Erichthonius, inventor of the four-horse chariot, or Myrtilus, charioteer of King Oenomaus.
Auriga.notable_features: Capella (6th brightest star), several open clusters including M36, M37, M38

Bootes.name: Boötes
Bootes.description: Boötes is a large constellation containing Arcturus, the brightest star in the northern celestial hemisphere.
Bootes.history: In Greek mythology, Boötes represents a herdsman or ploughman. Some legends associate him with Arcas, son of Zeus and Callisto.
Bootes.notable_features: Arcturus (4th brightest star overall), kite-shaped pattern
